name: Anchor-2D-GS / Anchor-3D-GS
text:
# Anchor-2D-GS / Anchor-3D-GS
Also called: Anchor-GS, modified versions of 2D-GS and 3D-GS

## Overview
Anchor-2D-GS and Anchor-3D-GS are modified variants of 2D-GS [15] and 3D-GS [5] that employ an anchor grid structure to organize Gaussian primitives more efficiently, reducing redundancy and storage overhead [S1]. They achieve competitive rendering quality with fewer file storage than original methods, demonstrating that the anchor design organizes primitives more efficiently [S1].

## How it works
**Inputs and Outputs:**
Input: Sparse [Structure-from-Motion (SfM)](#16341-structure-from-motion-sfm.md) points [S1]. Output: A set of 2D or 3D Gaussians organized within an anchor grid structure [S1].

**Data Structures:**
The method voxelize the input SfM points to create anchors [S1]. Each anchor is assigned 2D or 3D Gaussians [S1]. The exact layout of Gaussian attributes (fields, sizes, [bit packing](#21948-bit-packing.md)) is Not given in the sources, but follows the standard definitions of the parent method with spatial distribution constrained by the anchor grid [S1].

**Numbered Steps:**
1. Voxelize the input SfM points to generate the anchor grid [S1].
2. Assign 2D or 3D Gaussians to each anchor [S1].
3. Optimize the Gaussian parameters using the specified loss functions and [densification strategy](#15375-point-densification.md) [S1].

**Formulas:**
For Anchor-3D-GS, standard L1 and SSIM losses are used [S1]. For Anchor-2D-GS, the distortion loss is $L_d = \sum_{i,j} \omega_i \omega_j |z_i - z_j|$ and the normal loss is $L_n = \sum_i \omega_i (1 - \mathbf{n}_i^T \mathbf{N})$, where $\omega_i$ and $\omega_j$ are opacities, $z_i$ and $z_j$ are depths, $\mathbf{n}_i$ is the predicted normal, and $\mathbf{N}$ is the target normal [S1].

**Parameters:**
Voxel size for the anchor grid is 0.001 for all scenes [S1]. Training runs for 40k iterations with densification concluding at 20k iterations for standard scenes, or 100k iterations with densification ending at 50k iterations for large-scale scenes [S1]. The densification interval is $T = 100$ [S1]. The visibility threshold is $\tau_v = 0.7$ for small-scale scenes [S1]. Loss weights are 0.8 (L1) and 0.2 (SSIM) for Anchor-3D-GS, and 0.01 (distortion) and 0.05 (normal) for Anchor-2D-GS [S1].

**Edge Cases and Pitfalls:**
The method assumes the input consists of SfM points [S1]. Not all layers are fully densified during [progressive training](#9142-progressive-training.md), which may require extending densification by an additional 10k iterations [S1].

## Subtopics

### Anchor Gaussian Handling
Anchor Gaussians are hypothesized to constrain and regularize parameters of coarser-level Gaussians, typically having larger scales than regular Gaussians [S2]. They do not have actual opacity for rendering; for visualization, their opacity is manually set to $\text{sigmoid}(1)$ [S2]. The average scale of anchors is $e^{-5.08}$ across 100 randomly sampled scenes, while the average scale of Gaussians is $e^{-7.12}$ [S2]. This size difference suggests that Gaussians adjust their scales to represent sharp details in real-world images, whereas anchor Gaussians serve a regularization role [S2].

## Operating characteristics
The method achieves fewer file storage than original 2D-GS and 3D-GS methods [S1]. It delivers competitive rendering quality compared to original methods [S1]. The anchor design creates a more [compact representation](#1349-ssvdag-node-layout-and-tagged-pointer-encoding.md) by reducing redundancy [S1]. While Anchor-2D/3D-GS reduce storage, Octree-GS delivers better visual performance and fewer Gaussian primitives due to its explicit, multi-level anchor design [S1].

## Background
Introduced in Octree-GS [S1], the method modifies 2D-GS [15] and 3D-GS [5] by voxelizing input SfM points into an anchor grid and assigning Gaussians to each anchor, while adopting [Scaffold-GS](#9186-scaffold-gs.md)'s densification strategy [S1].

## Sources
[S1] Octree-GS: Towards Consistent Real-time Rendering with LOD-Structured 3D Gaussians, https://doi.org/10.1109/tpami.2025.3568201, fetched 2026-10-27
[S2] GSGAN: Adversarial Learning for Hierarchical Generation of 3D Gaussian Splats, https://doi.org/10.52202/079017-2171, fetched 2026-10-29
